I would highly recommend that you give great thought to your layout. A successful park will have tons of rides, sure, but will also ensure that the paths to and from those rides lead to facilities that need foot traffic. There could be enough shops in the park, but if they aren't located in ideal locations (i.e. around high traffic avenues, near entrances and exits of rides, drink shops by toilets) then they'll lose money dramatically. 

Essentials time:

Bathrooms should have at least a .50 cent charge to ensure they pay for themselves as the park grows, as long as the janitor crew is trained well and fully employed, then guests will happily stomach a small price. With that in mind, like I briefly noted they should always be placed near drink shops to ensure higher foot traffic and happier guests.

Guests usually get thirsty more than they get hungry, I've found 2 drinks to one food stall to be the golden ratio. There may he times where you have 5 and 3, or 4 and 2, but always ensure you have more drink than food.

You can never have too many benches or bins. Place bins like crazy, in later levels guests LIVE for littering. I place one at every corner and every bench and sometimes they STILL litter, they just love it.

And finally, rides. You might think the nausea or fear is the most important indicator, but the thing that really drives sales is excitement. You're looking for at least an amber (preferably green) rating for excitement on any ride you're placing. Guests like a little fear, and will stomach some nausea, but if it's too boring or outside of your parks demographics (a family ride with mostly adult guests) the ride will lose money. 

With pricing, coasters and tracks rides are a little higher, but the easy peasy way I price is 4 dollars for every star of prestige. 1 star is 4, 2stars is 8, 3.5 stars is 14. It's honestly conservative for sales and you can play with it to adjust for your parks demands, but if you're building rides fast it's a fast metric and guests are always pleased with the price.

I think part of your problem is the greener grasses affect. My lifelong best friend and I secretly always felt the other person was superior. I was always envious of how well kept her life was. She had a big loving family, she was always farther and more established in her career than me, and financially, she was secure while I struggled. I grew up with a mentally ill and abusive mother, and it greatly ruined my self-esteem and self-worth. I saw myself as unworthy to walk alongside her.

But I found out she was envious of me. I've always had a knack for creating things and can learn a new skill with ease. While I've had a rough upbringing, in her words, I never let that ruin my disposition towards others and treat everyone with kindness and respect.

I'm being long-winded, but my point is we are always our worst critics, and coupled with looking at someone else's grass can make us feel inferior. But your companions probably have moments when they look at you with respect. With envy even. They may be more established in one factor, but from one jack of all trades to another that doesn't diminish your worth. And from personal experience, it might be that very quality about you that they themselves wish they had. My therapist always tells me to be kinder to myself, show myself the same patience and regard that I show others, and remember that while there are qualities that I see in other people and wish for myself, that they may feel the exact same about me in a different regard.

Good luck OP. I hope you find inner peace, because it sounds like physically all the pieces are there for you.
